meta.title: Kodiak: The Anchor Came In Short
meta.dek: The compression business has never been better. The first data-center anchor turned out to be six years on old engines, and since then the stock has traded like an AI-power stock. At $45, is the compressor franchise on sale, or is the power plan still priced too generously?
meta.type: Contracted infrastructure: contract gas compression plus behind-the-meter power
meta.stage: Mature compounder (compression) funding an early-growth power build

verdict.sentence: A best-in-class compression fleet is funding a power build whose first anchor came in at six years on existing engines, not ten on new turbines; at $45 the probability-weighted case pays [[pw_return]] a year against the 13% hurdle, so the selloff is close to an opportunity without yet being one.
verdict.breaks_if: credit-agreement leverage goes above 3.5× at the November or February print, or Kodiak issues primary equity to fund power. Then the build costs shareholders more than it earns, and 10 points move from the Base to the Bear.

call: Since September 16 Kodiak has fallen 22% while Archrock fell 6%. Three things did it. On September 21 the West Texas project that management had at limited notice to proceed was signed as a six-year, 76 MW deal served from the existing recip fleet, at an undisclosed price, and the stock lost 10% in four sessions while Archrock lost 3%. The ten-year Treasury went to 5.3%. And from October 14 Kodiak traded with the AI-power complex, as CoreWeave's bonds broke and Meta's spending outlook reopened the financing question; it fell 10% on October 22 alongside GE Vernova and Vistra. Compression, which earns most of the cash, had no news at all. The six-year term fails my first test as written, so I cut the Bull to 15% and take management's new-build economics out of the Base. What remains is a business compounding at about [[compounding]] a year at a flat multiple, 4.3 points of it the dividend, plus a power fleet priced near legacy rates. The price implies [[implied_bear]] Bear odds at a 10% discount rate; I assign 30%. That earns [[pw_return]], short of 13%, and the verb is probability-fragile: break-even Bear odds are [[breakeven_bear]]. Leverage at the Q3 print settles it.

tests.claim: That new-build power earns its cost of capital.
tests.test: by the Q4 print (late February 2027), a signed contract of seven years or longer for at least 100 MW of the turbine fleet on order (not the existing recips), with management stating returns at or above its 15% unlevered target.
tests.if_fail: move 10 points from Bull to Bear (PW EV [[test1.pw_ev]], [[test1.pw_return]]/yr) → **[[test1.verb]]**, entry [[test1.entry]]; the 1.8 GW order becomes a funding burden rather than an option.

tests.claim: That the build stays inside the balance sheet.
tests.test: credit-agreement leverage at or below 3.5× at both the Q3 (early November) and Q4 (February) prints, a FY2027 capex plan funded from discretionary cash flow, the ABL and notes, and no primary equity issued.
tests.if_fail: move 10 points from Base to Bear (PW EV [[test2.pw_ev]], [[test2.pw_return]]/yr) → **[[test2.verb]]**, entry [[test2.entry]]; the Outsider grade drops to Anti-Outsider for equity issued below May's $71.

tests.claim: That compression pricing holds at peak utilization.
tests.test: Q3 and Q4 revenue per horsepower up at least 3.5% year over year (≥$24.40 by Q4), utilization ≥97.5% and compression adjusted gross margin ≥69% despite lube oil.
tests.if_fail: Base cut to $60 on 2% a year of price and a 66% margin (PW EV [[test3.pw_ev]], [[test3.pw_return]]/yr) → **[[test3.verb]]**, entry [[test3.entry]].

return_math.price_implied: At a 10% discount rate, spot needs FY2031 owner cash flow of [[Priced-in.owner_eps]] a share ([[Priced-in.cagr]] a year on discretionary cash flow) at a 9.6× exit: about four-fifths of the way from the Bear to the Base.
return_math.epv: ≈$55 per share: FY2026 owner cash flow of ≈$5.5 a share (discretionary cash flow less SBC) capitalized at 10% with no growth. Spot is about $10 below EPV, so the price gives the power build a negative value: it assumes the ≈$4B still to be spent earns less than its cost. The Bear ($25) sits below EPV because it adds a gas downturn to a stalled build.
return_math.base_rate: The Bull needs ≈17% nominal (≈14% real) revenue growth for five years from $1.5B; in the nearest base-rate bucket about 12% of companies sustain ≥15% real. Possible, not probable, which is the tier I give it. The Base needs ≈9% nominal, about the median for this size.
return_math.year_ten: Compression still adds 3–4% a year while engine lead times stay long; power's runway past 2030 depends on behind-the-meter staying a data-center default once grid interconnects catch up. In the Base the 9.6× exit is doing modest work; in the Bull most of the value is the power fleet's re-contracting.
